PullRequest.Title: launch skill: record Code OSS demo videos and fix Windows cleanup
PullRequest.Body:
﻿<!-- Thank you for submitting a Pull Request. Please:
* Read our Pull Request guidelines:
  https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/wiki/How-to-Contribute#pull-requests
* Associate an issue with the Pull Request.
* Ensure that the code is up-to-date with the `main` branch.

This updates the `launch` skill so agents can record a demo video of Code OSS and clean up reliably on Windows. It is intended to be used together with a general Playwright video-recording skill, such as the Team Tools `record-video` skill (https://github.com/microsoft/vscode-packages/pull/381). This skill only covers what is specific to Code OSS.

## Changes

- **Recording a video**: a new section explains how to use the attached `@playwright/cli` session as the Playwright `page` for `page.screencast`:
  - Run the whole scenario, from `start()` to `stop()`, as one `run-code --filename` call.
  - Keep typed text short. Typing into Monaco key by key is slow: one test typed about 400 characters and produced a nearly four-minute video.
  - Run commands by pressing `F1`, filling the Command Palette textbox, and clicking the exact matching option. Pressing `Enter` right after filling can run a stale result.
- **Sandboxed agent terminals**: Code OSS can't be launched from a sandboxed agent terminal. On Windows, the sandbox can't start at all unless local network access is enabled, and even with it enabled the launcher fails with `[launch.ps1] Access is denied`. The skill now tells the agent to request unsandboxed execution where its shell tool supports that. Otherwise it should ask the user once, before launching, to turn off "Sandboxing for terminal" for the session, instead of suggesting that enabling local network access is enough.
- **Windows cleanup fix**: `cleanup.ps1` never matched the launched processes. The launcher passes `--user-data-dir` with `%TEMP%`'s short 8.3 form (`C:\Users\ABCDEF~1\...`). Windows PowerShell's `GetFullPath` expands the run directory to its long form, so the exact argument comparison always failed and the processes were never stopped. Cleanup now compares the directory both arguments refer to (via `GetLongPathName`).

## How to test

1. In an agent session in a compiled VS Code checkout, ask: *Record a short video of Code OSS built from this repository showing that "View: Toggle Word Wrap" wraps a long line in a new untitled file.*
2. If the terminal is sandboxed, the agent should ask once to turn off terminal sandboxing. It should then launch Code OSS, record a WebM into its session storage folder, and clean up the instance.

Tested on Windows (Insiders 1.143) with a fresh agent session. The agent discovered both skills on its own and recorded a 23-second WebM; its checks passed (1 row became 4 wrapped rows with the text unchanged). Cleanup removed its instance without manual steps. The new path matcher was also tested directly in Windows PowerShell 5.1 with short, long and unrelated paths. Not tested on macOS or Linux; the bash launcher and cleanup are unchanged.

RegressionFixes.Mechanism: The cleanup owner used a spelling-sensitive argument comparison and could lose the only targeted handle to still-running Electron processes when Windows represented the same temp directory in short versus long form, retaining the process tree and its 1-4 GB working set after the demo session.
RegressionFixes.Symptom: Windows launch sessions could survive cleanup indefinitely, retaining a full Code OSS Electron process tree and gigabytes of memory until manually terminated.
RegressionFixes.FixedBehavior: Cleanup now compares the canonical long form of the expected run directory and each `--user-data-dir` value, so short and long spellings select the launched Code OSS process and allow it to be terminated before deleting the profile.
RegressionFixes.Evidence: The base cleanup required an ordinal-insensitive exact `--user-data-dir=<path>` string match before every Stop-Process. The launcher derives that argument from `$env:TEMP` and returns `runDir`, while cleanup reparses the supplied runDir with GetFullPath; Windows short (8.3) and long spellings can therefore name the same directory without matching. The changed call at cleanup.ps1:44 delegates to a path-aware matcher that expands both spellings with GetLongPathName. If the old predicate misses, no Code OSS child is stopped; the documented cleanup path then attempts recursive deletion while the Electron instance remains live. Repository guidance identifies each instance as consuming 1-4 GB and explicitly requires cleanup.

Scenarios.Scenario: Clean up a launched Code OSS demo session on Windows
Scenarios.CriticalPath: After the demo, optional Playwright shutdown, process discovery/termination, and recursive run-directory removal must complete before cleanup returns. This is teardown rather than launch or interaction critical path.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Runs `npx @playwright/cli ... close` when a session name is supplied.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: At most one subprocess per cleanup invocation.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The same optional subprocess ran before this PR.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Cleanup waits for it, but failures are explicitly allowed to continue to process cleanup.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Queries Win32_Process through CIM/WMI and reads command lines.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One scan per termination attempt, up to five, plus one final verification scan; each scan covers the system process list, while path conversion is reached only for Code - OSS.exe entries with command lines.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The same number and placement of full process-list scans existed before the PR.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Each scan is synchronous on teardown; existing 500 ms waits dominate repeated successful termination attempts.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Compiles the NativePath C# interop helper with Add-Type.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: Once per cleanup PowerShell process; the type guard prevents recompilation if the helper is sourced again in the same process.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Cleanup already compiled one NativeCommandLine helper; it did not compile the additional NativePath helper.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Adds one bounded startup compilation to teardown only.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Calls GetLongPathName to canonicalize the expected local temp path and candidate user-data path.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: The expected path is converted once per Code OSS process tested, and a candidate is converted only for a matching `--user-data-dir` argument. With a normal Electron process tree this is a small bounded count per WMI scan; retries cease once no matching process remains.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Compared argument strings directly without path canonicalization, which could miss short/long aliases.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Synchronous but bounded path canonicalization during teardown; it enables process ownership matching and prevents leaked processes.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Recursively deletes the isolated run directory.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One successful recursive deletion, retried up to five times on failure.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The same deletion and retry loop existed, but a missed process could retain file handles and cause failure.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Cleanup waits for deletion; cost scales with copied profile size.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Cost scales with system process-list size for each WMI scan, number of Code OSS processes for path matching, and isolated-profile file count for deletion. The diff changes only the small per-Code-process canonicalization cost and makes teardown release matching processes.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Cleanup is serial: it closes one Playwright session, performs up to five WMI process scans with serial Stop-Process calls and 500 ms waits, performs one final scan, then retries recursive deletion serially. The changed matcher does not add parallel work.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: No cache participates. Native helper types are reused only within the one PowerShell process; every cleanup invocation performs fresh process discovery and path conversion.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: changed-line and caller tracing establish the serial invocation counts and cleanup lifecycle. The short/long path mismatch mechanism is directly addressed by canonicalizing both sides.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Exact Add-Type and GetLongPathName latency varies by Windows host, but both are one-shot teardown work and small relative to WMI scans, waits, and recursive deletion. The removed leak can retain 1-4 GB per documented Code OSS instance.
Scenarios.Verdict: No reportable regression. The added bounded teardown work fixes a cleanup-lifecycle resource leak; the fixing regression was recorded internally.

Scenarios.Scenario: Record a Code OSS demo video through the attached Playwright page
Scenarios.CriticalPath: A single run-code invocation starts screencast, performs the scripted UI scenario, and stops recording; all scripted interaction and recording duration are on the video-generation critical path.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Runs one `npx @playwright/cli ... run-code --filename=<file>` process for the complete recording scenario.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: Exactly one CLI subprocess per recommended recording scenario rather than splitting start, actions, and stop across multiple invocations.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The launch skill had no Code OSS-specific video-recording workflow; ordinary UI instructions used separate CLI commands.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: The process remains active for the recording and must reach stop before the video is complete.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Drives the attached workbench page over the existing local Playwright/CDP session and receives screencast frames.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One attached session; interaction messages scale with scenario actions and key-by-key typing, while frame traffic scales with recording duration/frame rate.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The skill documented Playwright attachment and interaction but not screencast use of that page.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Required recording work; typing and interactions extend video duration directly.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: The external recording workflow writes the resulting video file.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One output video whose bytes scale with duration, frame rate, dimensions, and visual changes.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: No video output was prescribed by this launch skill.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Recording cannot complete until screencast stop/finalization; exact implementation belongs to the referenced general recording workflow, not changed repository code.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: CPU, encoded bytes, and elapsed time scale with recording duration and frame count; Monaco interaction time scales with typed character count. The added guidance explicitly bounds typed text and recommends pasting long setup before recording.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: One attached Playwright page executes one async scenario serially. Screencast capture may encode frames concurrently inside Playwright/browser internals, but this documentation change adds no application-side fan-out or queue.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: No repository cache is changed. `npx` may use an already installed local devDependency; cold package resolution is environment-dependent, but the instructions use one invocation and do not add repeated resolution.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High for the documented one-process/one-session workflow; moderate for exact encoding cost because page.screencast implementation is external and unchanged here.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Encoding parameters and scenario duration are external to this diff. The documented 400-character example demonstrates why the guidance avoids long key-by-key input, but no changed runtime implementation forces that workload.
Scenarios.Verdict: No reportable regression. Video capture necessarily incurs duration-proportional work, and the new guidance reduces invocation overhead and warns users away from the known character-scaling interaction.

Scenarios.Scenario: Launch and drive Code OSS when the agent terminal is sandboxed
Scenarios.CriticalPath: The new instruction moves launcher, Playwright CLI, and cleanup execution to an unsandboxed terminal context so launch can proceed; it changes execution permissions, not the launcher implementation or its workload.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Starts the existing launcher, Playwright CLI, and cleanup commands outside terminal sandboxing.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: The same command count as the corresponding launch/drive/cleanup workflow.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: These subprocesses already formed the workflow; the documentation did not correctly require an execution context in which Windows launch succeeds.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Avoids a failed sandboxed launch and retry; no new subprocess is added.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: No collection or history scaling is introduced; cost remains one launch workflow per session.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Unchanged: one launcher instance and one attached Playwright session per documented demo workflow.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High that no executable code or boundary cardinality changes in this scenario.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Host sandbox implementations vary, but this is documentation-only routing and does not add runtime work.
Scenarios.Verdict: No performance regression. The instruction avoids failed launch attempts rather than adding work.

Analysis.Summary: Completed the performance pass over all three changed files and every diff hunk. Traced Windows cleanup, video recording, and sandboxed launch scenarios through subprocess, WMI/IPC, native path, and filesystem boundaries. No diff-introduced actionable performance issue was found; the Windows matcher instead fixes a concrete cleanup-lifecycle memory leak, recorded with its blamed introducing commit.

Stats.CostNote: Copilot SDK reports nano-AI units and model billing multipliers; it does not provide a USD conversion.
